papers.title: Striatal network dysfunction underlying speech impairment in early Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: The pathophysiology underlying Parkinson's disease (PD) speech impairments and its potential sex differences remain unclear. We investigated sex-specific alterations in speech and striato-cortical networks in 104 patients with early PD (68M/36F), and 44 healthy controls (23M/21F), using quantitative speech markers and multimodal neuroimaging. Speech features related to prosody, phonation, articulation, fluency, and rhythm, were extracted from voice recordings; striatal dopaminergic loss was quantified using DaT-SPECT, and functional connectivity between striatal and cortical language networks was analyzed with resting-state fMRI. Results showed that PD-related speech impairments were more pronounced in males. Functional connectivity was globally reduced in PD, but female patients exhibited higher caudate-cortical connectivity. In males, speech deficits were associated with both dopaminergic loss and connectivity disruption, whereas in females, only connectivity changes were involved. These findings revealed sex-specific pathophysiological mechanisms in early PD speech disorders, emphasizing the need for sex-stratified approaches in research and clinical practice.

papers.title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34-45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. papers.title: A deep learning-based silhouette gait detection framework for fall risk classification in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a rapidly growing neurodegenerative disorder associated with gait impairment, functional decline, and increased fall risk. Conventional clinical assessments rely heavily on brief observational scales and are limited by subjectivity and environmental bias. There is a pressing need for objective, quantitative, and scalable digital assessment tools to support precision management of PD. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to develop and validate a smartphone-video-based gait assessment system aligned with a clinically meaningful pathway encompassing PD screening, functional evaluation, and fall risk classification. METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, patients with mild-to-moderate PD and age-matched healthy controls were recruited following Institutional Review Board approval. Gait videos were recorded using smartphone cameras and processed through a silhouette extraction pipeline. Spatiotemporal gait features were subsequently extracted using a MoviNet-based deep learning framework. A multi-task framework was developed to perform PD screening, activities of daily living functional grading based on the Schwab and England Activities of Daily Living (S&E ADL) scale, and fall risk classification. Model performance and generalizability were evaluated using subject-independent data partitioning and independent cross-site validation. RESULTS: A total of 40 participants were recruited. For PD screening, the model achieved an accuracy of 95.7%, a sensitivity of 96.6%, a specificity of 92.2%, and an AUC of 0.994 on the independent test set. For S&E ADL functional grading, the model achieved an overall accuracy of 88.5% across three functional categories (80, 90, and 100%). For fall risk classification, the model achieved an accuracy of 91.1%, a sensitivity of 68.4%, a specificity of 98.3%, and an AUC of 0.909. papers.title: Neurofilament Light Chain and Mutant Huntingtin Across Huntington's Disease Integrated Staging System Stages in Huntington Disease: A Cross-Sectional Multimodal Analysis.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Huntington's Disease Integrated Staging System (HD-ISS) provides a framework for staging HD but does not incorporate fluid biomarkers. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to examine neurofilament light chain (NfL) and mutant huntingtin (mHTT) and total tau across HD-ISS stages and their associations with genetic burden, neuroimaging, and clinical measures. METHODS: We performed cross-sectional analysis of the Barcelona-Huntington's Disease (BCN-HD) cohort with external replication in the multicenter HDClarity study. HD gene expansion carriers were classified as HD-ISS stages 0 to 3. NfL (cerebrospinal fluid [CSF] and plasma), CSF mHTT, total tau, striatal volumes, and Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale measures were quantified. Group differences and associations were analyzed using adjusted models. RESULTS: The BCN-HD cohort included 78 participants (50 HD gene expansion carriers [HDGECs], 28 controls) and HDClarity included 218 participants (166 HDGECs, 52 controls). CSF NfL increased across HD-ISS stages and discriminated premanifest from manifest individuals, as well as HD-ISS stage 0 from stage 1. Plasma NfL showed parallel increases and strongly correlated with CSF NfL (ρ = 0.88, P < 0.001). More than half of HD-ISS 0 individuals had NfL levels above the age-adjusted 95th percentile (P95) and shorter predicted time to onset (13 years for CSF and 10 years for plasma). From HD-ISS 1 onward, NfL levels exceeded P95 in most individuals. Higher NfL concentrations were associated with genetic burden, striatal atrophy, and clinical measures (all P < 0.001). CSF mHTT was detectable from HD-ISS 0 but showed weaker associations, whereas CSF total tau increased only from HD-ISS 3. CONCLUSIONS: NfL identifies biological activity across the HD-ISS continuum and shows neuroaxonal injury in a subset of individuals classified as stage 0. papers.title: HMGB1 functional plasticity in neurodegenerative diseases and its translational implications.
papers.abstract: High mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) is a chromatin-associated protein that can be redistributed and released during cellular stress, when it acts as an extracellular alarmin within the broader family of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Its functions depend on subcellular localization, redox and post-translational modification state, cellular source, mode of release, and molecular partners. This critical narrative review examines how these variables shape HMGB1 biology in Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Huntington's disease (HD), spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and related disorders, and considers their implications for biomarker and therapeutic development. Intracellular HMGB1 contributes to chromatin organization, DNA repair, mitochondrial genome maintenance, and proteostasis. After redistribution and release, extracellular HMGB1 signals through receptors including the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), interacts with disease-associated proteins, and links proteostatic stress with glial activation, neuronal dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier impairment. Across disease models, two recurrent patterns emerge: loss or sequestration of intracellular HMGB1 in models of polyglutamine disorders, including HD and SCAs, and extracellular HMGB1 signaling as a progression-associated inflammatory amplifier in AD, PD, and ALS models. Central-peripheral inflammatory communication and cell-specific HMGB1 release further shape these responses. Clinical studies have associated total HMGB1 or anti-HMGB1 autoantibodies with clinical features, but current assays do not resolve redox form, cellular source, or biological activity. Most therapeutic studies remain preclinical, while available human intervention studies involve drugs with multiple molecular actions. papers.title: Deficiency of Synaptotagmin 9 in the Hippocampal Region Induces Synaptic Damage and Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson's Disease Mice via BDNF/TrkB Signaling.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a prominent non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD) that severely affects patients' quality of life, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of hippocampal Synaptotagmin 9 (Syt9) in PD-related cognitive deficits. We found that Syt9 expression was significantly downregulated in the hippocampus of both MPTP-induced subacute PD mice and A53T α-synuclein transgenic mice, concomitant with cognitive impairment and synaptic damage. To determine causality, we performed hippocampal Syt9 knockdown and overexpression using AAV-mediated gene delivery. Syt9 knockdown exacerbated, while Syt9 overexpression alleviated, cognitive deficits and synaptic structural abnormalities in PD mice. Proteomic sequencing and pharmacological manipulations revealed that Syt9 may regulate the BDNF/TrkB signaling pathway at the protein level, likely by influencing BDNF vesicular transport, release, or stability. Intra-hippocampal BDNF supplementation rescued synaptic damage and cognitive impairment, whereas the TrkB antagonist ANA-12 reversed the protective effects of Syt9 overexpression. Collectively, our findings identify the Syt9/BDNF/TrkB axis as a key mechanism in PD-related cognitive impairment and suggest that targeting this pathway may offer a novel therapeutic strategy for PD.

papers.title: Restoring Neural Homeostasis via Class II HDAC Modulation: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.abstract: Class II histone deacetylases (HDACs) comprise class IIa enzymes HDAC4, HDAC5, HDAC7, and HDAC9 and class IIb enzymes HDAC6 and HDAC10, which differ substantially in structure, catalytic activity, subcellular localization, and neural function. Class IIa HDACs exhibit weak intrinsic deacetylase activity and function predominantly as signal-responsive scaffolds that couple calcium and kinase signaling to transcription through nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, recruitment of HDAC3-containing NCoR/SMRT corepressor complexes, and interactions with MEF2, CREB, and FOXO. Conversely, HDAC6 is a predominantly cytoplasmic deacetylase that regulates α-tubulin acetylation, cytoskeletal dynamics, axonal transport, autophagy, and proteostasis. Dysregulated class II HDAC signaling contributes to neurodegenerative diseases through convergent mechanisms involving synaptic dysfunction, maladaptive transcriptional repression, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and defective clearance of pathological proteins. Disease-associated substrates include amyloid-β and tau in Alzheimer's disease, α-synuclein in Parkinson's disease, mutant huntingtin in Huntington's disease, and TDP-43/SOD1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Emerging evidence additionally links aberrant HDAC4/5 signaling to neurodevelopmental disorders through altered synaptic maturation, excitation-inhibition balance, and circuit development. This review integrates the structural and mechanistic biology of class II HDACs with their disease-specific roles and evaluates therapeutic approaches to restore neural homeostasis. Particular emphasis is placed on selective HDAC6 inhibitors, modulation of class IIa protein-protein interactions and subcellular trafficking, natural compounds, and RNA-based strategies. papers.title: Disarming CH25H to clear α-synuclein.
papers.abstract: α-Synuclein (α-Syn) accumulation is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD). Zhang et al. identify cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (CH25H) as an astrocytic inhibitor of p62-dependent α-Syn degradation. Disrupting the CH25H-p62 interaction facilitates α-Syn clearance via autophagy and improves PD-like phenotypes, suggesting a previously unrecognized nonenzymatic function for CH25H with therapeutic potential.

papers.title: The small giant actor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases: Microtubules.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a clinically and pathologically diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuronal loss. Although research has traditionally focused on disease-associated protein misfolding and aggregation, increasing evidence implicates abnormalities of cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport in several neurodegenerative conditions. Microtubules contribute to neuronal polarity, axonal and dendritic transport, organelle distribution, and synaptic maintenance. These functions are regulated in part by tubulin isotypes, post-translational modifications collectively described as the tubulin code, microtubule-associated proteins, and molecular motors. This narrative review examines evidence linking alterations in these processes with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease. We summarize proposed interactions among microtubule instability, impaired axonal transport, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disease-associated proteins, including tau, α-synuclein, mutant huntingtin, TDP-43, and prion protein. Evidence connecting tau pathology with microtubule dysfunction is comparatively well established in Alzheimer's disease and MAPT-related tauopathies, whereas findings in other disorders are more heterogeneous and are frequently derived from cellular or animal models. We also discuss emerging experimental approaches, candidate biomarkers, and investigational microtubule-directed treatments. However, no tubulin-specific biomarker or microtubule-targeted disease-modifying treatment discussed in this review has yet been clinically validated. Overall, microtubule dysfunction may represent one component of broader, disease-specific pathological networks rather than a universal primary cause of neurodegeneration. papers.title: Trans-Vatabnet: Transcriptomic Signatures For Parkinson's Disease Detection Using Deep Learning.
papers.abstract: The early detection of Parkinson's disease (PD) is critical for timely and effective clinical intervention and disease management. High dimensional gene expression data redundancy features, class imbalance and limited interpretability are challenges discussed for transcriptomic-based diagnostic approaches. To overcome these drawbacks, TransVaTabNet, new approach that combines transcriptomic analysis, deep learning and explainable artificial intelligence detect PD and discover biomarkers. The RNA-seq data is first pre-processed by low expression gene filtering, Trimmed Mean of M-values normalization, and voom transformation. The differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are determined through the framework of Limma-voom, and are then subjected to stage-specific gene analysis and functional enrichment to map the disease-related biological pathways. The high dimensional gene expression profiles are learned to a compact latent representation using a Variational AutoEncoder, and SMOTE is used to deal with class imbalance. The derived features are then classified with a TabNet model that adopts a sequential attention mechanism to attend to informative transcriptomic patterns. In addition, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used for model interpretability and biomarker identification. Experimental results on the GSE216281 RNA-seq dataset are shown to validate the proposed framework with 90.95% Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), outperforming the classical machine learning models. The results show that TransVaTabNet can provide an accurate, interpretable and biologically meaningful framework for stage-specific detection PD and biomarker discovery, which can support precision diagnosis and further clinical decisions.

papers.title: Pleiotrophin: a multifunctional regulator in neurodevelopment and neuropsychiatric diseases.
papers.abstract: Pleiotrophin (PTN) is a heparin-binding growth factor that plays a pivotal role in neurodevelopment, neuroplasticity, and neuroinflammation. PTN signals through a multi-receptor network involving protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type ζ (PTPRZ1), syndecans (particularly syndecan-3), integrins, nucleolin, and neuropilin-1. Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) has also been functionally linked to PTN signaling, although whether PTN directly binds and activates it remains debated. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in understanding the structure, distribution, and multifunctional roles of PTN in the nervous system, with a particular focus on its involvement in neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, anxiety, depression, and schizophrenia. Emerging evidence suggests that PTN exhibits context-dependent and often dual roles, both neuroprotective and pathogenic, depending on the disease stage and cellular microenvironment. This review highlights the potential of PTN as well as its receptors as therapeutic targets and underscores the direction for further research to elucidate its precise mechanisms in neurological and psychiatric conditions.

papers.title: How do neurorehabilitation patients perceive their fundamental care needs? Findings from a qualitative study.
papers.journal: PM & R : the journal of injury, function, and rehabilitation
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Fundamentals of Care (FoC) framework provides a structured model to support the delivery of person-centered nursing care by integrating physical, psychosocial, and relational dimensions. Although the framework has been widely applied in acute care, little is known about its relevance in long-term neurorehabilitation settings, where patients often face complex, prolonged, and multidimensional care needs. OBJECTIVE: To explore how individuals with neurological disorders perceive their fundamental care needs during inpatient rehabilitation. DESIGN: A qualitative secondary analysis. SETTING: A rehabilitation hospital in Italy with a total capacity of 109 beds. PARTICIPANTS: We recruited individuals aged 18 years and older with a diagnosis of stroke, multiple sclerosis, or Parkinson disease, or who had undergone neurosurgical intervention for oncological conditions. METHODS: A deductive content analysis was performed, using the FoC framework to guide coding and thematic development. FINDINGS: The analysis identified care experiences across the three FoC dimensions. In the physical dimension, patients valued hygiene, toileting, mobility, and comfort not only as technical tasks but also as meaningful acts that contributed to dignity and recovery. The psychosocial dimension emphasized the importance of respectful communication, emotional support, privacy, and being informed, factors that fostered agency and trust. In the relational dimension, patients highlighted empathy, continuity, and presence as central to feeling emotionally safe and supported. Health care assistants emerged as key figures in delivering comfort-focused and relational care. Across all dimensions, fundamental care was perceived as deeply interconnected and resistant to rigid, task-based models. papers.title: Quantitative Evaluation of Respiratory Dysfunction and Its Relationships With Parkinson's Disease Symptoms.
papers.abstract: Respiratory disorders significantly impair functional baseline and quality of life (QoL) in Parkinson's disease (PD). This cross-sectional study aimed to evaluate spirographic lung function parameters in PD and determine their relationships with motor and nonmotor symptoms, QoL, and dopaminergic therapy. Spirometric parameters were recorded in 57 outpatients with PD and 10 healthy controls. PD patients underwent clinical assessments using UPDRS Parts II and III, Schwab and England scale, PDQ-39, and PFS-16. Spirometric analysis revealed significant decreases in VC %pred in PD patients versus controls, and in FVC %pred in PD Stage III versus PD Stage II. papers.title: Effects of Exercise Training on the Metabolic Cost of Walking in Health and Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The metabolic cost of walking (Cw) increases with heathy aging and in neurological conditions. No comprehensive assessment has been performed yet to determine whether chronic exercise training and rehabilitation could improve Cw. OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to determine whether the effects of chronic exercise interventions on Cw differ by type, dose, and intensity in healthy adults and individuals with neurological conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and stroke). DESIGN: Systematic review and robust variance estimation meta-analysis with meta-regression following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. DATA SOURCES: Systematic search of Medline, Web of Science, and CINAHL databases. RESULTS: A total of 27 studies with 36 intervention arms and 54 outcomes in 1177 participants, of those 703 healthy adults and 474 patients with multiple sclerosis (1 study), Parkinson's disease (1 study), and stroke (9 studies) were included. Across all types of training (aerobic, resistance, other), chronic physical exercise training improved Cw (g = 0.40, p = 0.001). Improvements were significant in healthy individuals (g = 0.49, p = 0.001) but not in patients with stroke (g = 0.24, p = 0.065). Meta-regression confirmed that population moderated the effects of training on Cw (p = 0.043) after adjusting for exercise training characteristics. In the adjusted meta-regression, higher study-level mean body mass index (BMI) was associated with smaller intervention effects on Cw (β = - 0.20, p = 0.040). Training type, duration, intensity, frequency, and session duration did not significantly moderate the training effects on Cw, although the meta-regression may have been underpowered to detect such associations. papers.title: Marked intrafamilial phenotypic heterogeneity associated with the CSF1R c.2539G>A pathogenic variant in a Japanese family.
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in the colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) gene cause CSF1R-related disorder (CSF1R-RD), which encompasses a broad phenotypic spectrum including a classical adult-onset leukoencephalopathy phenotype. Within this spectrum, considerable phenotypic heterogeneity has been increasingly recognized. The pathogenic missense variant c.2539G>A has been reported in a small number of patients with CSF1R-associated leukoencephalopathy; however, its associated clinical spectrum remains incompletely characterized. To characterize the clinical spectrum associated with the CSF1R c.2539G>A pathogenic variant in a Japanese family with CSF1R-RD. Clinical evaluations and genetic analyses, including whole-exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing, were performed in available family members. We detected the same heterozygous CSF1R c.2539G>A pathogenic variant in four members from a Japanese family. Two affected individuals presented with parkinsonism, cognitive decline, and white matter abnormalities typical of CSF1R-RD, whereas the other affected individual exhibited a phenotype consistent with typical Parkinson's disease (PD), without apparent cognitive impairment or radiological white matter abnormalities. The fourth individual initially had no overt neurological symptoms despite white matter changes on MRI and subsequently developed spastic gait with pyramidal signs, indicating intrafamilial phenotypic variability. These findings broaden the phenotypic spectrum associated with the CSF1R c.2539G>A pathogenic variant and highlight marked intrafamilial phenotypic heterogeneity, including a PD-like phenotype without typical cognitive or white matter abnormalities.

papers.title: Prevalence and Associations of Abnormal Levels of Vitamin B6 in People with Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: In people with Parkinson's disease, abnormal levels of vitamin B6 may be associated with polyneuropathy and epileptic seizures, including medication-refractory status epilepticus. OBJECTIVES: To estimate the prevalence and explore associations of abnormal levels of vitamin B6 in people with Parkinson's disease. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, fasting serum levels of vitamin B6 and related metabolites were measured in 144 people with Parkinson's disease randomly recruited from eligible clinic patients, compared with 144 historical controls matched for age, sex, diet, and vitamin supplementation. Mixed-effects logistic regression was used to compare the prevalences of abnormal B6 levels, and mixed-effects analysis of variance was used to compare mean B6 levels between groups. Mixed effects regression models were used to examine associations between B6 levels and pre-defined demographic and clinical variables. RESULTS: Mean age was 71 years (range = 43-87) and 38.2% were female. Almost all were treated with carbidopa/levodopa (n = 140/144, mean levodopa dosage = 800 mg/day, mean treatment duration = 78 months). The prevalence of B6 deficiency in people with Parkinson's disease was 36.1% compared to 4.9% in controls (OR = 11.4, 95% CI = 4.9-26.5, p < 0.001). The average B6 level in people with Parkinson's disease was approximately half of that in controls (ratio of geometric means = 0.49, 95% CI = 0.41-0.58, p < 0.001). The severity of levodopa-associated motor complications (p = 0.04) and the presence of epileptic seizures (p = 0.006) were associated with lower log-transformed B6 levels. papers.title: Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 is involved in the microtubule-mediated regulation of intraocular pressure.
papers.journal: The Journal of pharmacology and experimental therapeutics
papers.abstract: Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) is known as the most common gene responsible for familial Parkinson disease (PD). This protein plays a key role in the neurodegenerative pathways associated with PD. LRRK2 also plays critical roles in actin dynamics and microtubule cytoskeletal assembly in the cells. In addition to PD, actin and microtubule cytoskeletons are associated with the onset and development of glaucoma by regulating the intraocular pressure (IOP) in humans and animals. However, the role of LRRK2 in regulating IOP remains unclear. Hence, this study investigated the contribution of LRRK2 to cytoskeleton-mediated regulation of IOP. LRRK2 was detected in primary human trabecular meshwork cells by immunofluorescence and western blotting analysis. Inhibition of the function and the expression of LRRK2 by LRRK2 inhibitors and LRRK2 siRNA, induced a significant reduction of TEER in these cells. TEER reduction by an LRRK2 inhibitor was attenuated by paclitaxel, a-tubulin polymerization inducer, but not by jasplakinolide, an actin polymerization inducer, suggesting that inhibition of LRRK2 induced depolymerization of microtubules, resulting in decreased TEER. Finally, LRRK2 gene knockout and LRRK2 inhibition led to a significant reduction of IOP in C57BL6J mice and Japanese white rabbits, respectively. These results suggested that LRRK2 is associated with catalysis of a-tubulin in trabecular meshwork cells and regulates IOP in mice and rabbits. Hence, there is a possibility that an LRRK2 inhibitor contributes to glaucoma therapeutics. Further evaluation to clarify the role of LRRK2 in IOP regulation is needed. papers.title: GCH1 p.Ser80Asn Confers Risk for Parkinson's Disease in East Asian Populations.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: GCH1 has been implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), but its risks variants and associations are not well defined. OBJECTIVES: Our goal was to investigate the clinical relevance and PD risk associated with the GCH1 p.Ser80Asn variant. METHODS: We first identified a segregating GCH1 p.Ser80Asn variant in a Malaysian Chinese PD family via whole genome sequencing (WGS). papers.title: Generation of a CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic control iPSC line (NIMHi001-A-1) from a Parkinson's disease Patient-Derived iPSC line carrying the LRRK2 I1371V mutation.
papers.abstract: We report NIMHi001-A-1, a CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic iPSC line derived from a patient line carrying a heterozygous LRRK2 missense mutation GRCh38 chr12:g.40308618A > G [(MANE transcript NM_198578.4:c.4111A > G); p.Ile1371Val] associated with familial Parkinson's disease. Sanger sequencing confirmed successful correction. The line retained iPSC morphology and expressed pluripotency markers (OCT4, NANOG, SOX2, TRA-1-60, SSEA4) by immunofluorescence, gene expression analysis, and flow cytometry. Normal karyotype (46, XY) and complete genetic identity with the parental line were established by STR profiling. No off-target modifications were detected. The line demonstrated trilineage differentiation potential and tested negative for mycoplasma, providing an isogenic platform to investigate LRRK2 I1371V-specific pathomechanisms and evaluate therapeutic strategies.
